1:
Job turns from his appeal to heaven to the wreck of his own body, and the witnesses gather about a dying man taking the inventory of himself. The reformed John Gill hears in "my breath is corrupt" the work of the disease that had made Job's very breath strange and disagreeable, even to his wife; the word carries the sense of pain, of the pangs of a woman in travail, so that Job draws each breath with labour, like one troubled with an asthma or fetching his last gasp. Yet Gill allows the term may be rendered "my spirit," the vital spirits now all but spent, or "my mind," the soul so overwhelmed with grief that he was scarce himself, distracted with the terrors of God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the philology against the harsher guess: chubbal means not to be destroyed but to be corrupted and troubled, and the word is best taken of the breath, grown short and offensive, announcing suffocation and decay no longer far off. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, refers the corrupt breath to the very symptom of elephantiasis, though he notes the margin's "my spirit is consumed."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole verse as a man correcting himself. He had said, in ch. 16:22, that when a few years were come he should go that long journey; now he sees he is already setting out, ready to be offered, the time of his departure at hand. Our life is going, Henry says, for the breath of life is continually going forth; our time is ending, our days extinct, put out like a candle that from its first lighting is always wasting toward the socket; and we are expected in our long home, for "the graves are ready." Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley both hear in the plural "graves" the sepulchres of Job's fathers, to which he must be gathered — a bed soon made, and if it be ready for us, it concerns us to be ready for it. The other wesleyan voice, Adam Clarke, renders the line "my spirit is oppressed" and points the second clause at the burial-niches of an ancient cemetery, "the sepulchral cells are ready for me." Ellicott adds that the plural is only the Hebrew idiom that uses the plural for the singular, as with the word blood: the grave, singular, is Job's portion. The voices divide gently over the words — a corrupted breath or a consumed spirit, the tombs of the fathers or a plain plural — but converge on the man, who has done with the world and has nothing left to wish for but a grave.
2:
From the grave he has just named Job turns back to the living who will not leave him in peace, and the witnesses take up a verse whose very words the translators could scarcely agree upon. The reformed John Gill is content with the plain sense: the "mockers" are not profane scoffers at religion but Job's own friends, whom he felt to be scorners of his misery, and it is because he is thus surrounded that he begs his cause be heard. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way — do not my friends, instead of comforting me, mock me? — and hears Job returning to the complaint of ch. 16:20 to justify the appeal that follows.

The grammatical-historical voices weigh the wording more warily. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "truly mockery surrounds me, and mine eye shall loiter over their disputings," and defend the chapter-division here against those who would move it: the thought of ch. 16:22 is a true conclusion, and a fresh strain begins, the lines moving crosswise, so that this verse of mockery leads on to the plea for a surety in the next. Charles Ellicott glosses "mine eye continue in their provocation" as a bitter reproach: the eye sees, and can see nothing else, having nothing else to look upon but the taunts of his comforters.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays the difficulty bare, running through the renderings the verse has borne — the Vulgate's "I have not sinned, and yet mine eye dwells upon afflictions," the Septuagint's talk of strangers robbing him of his substance, Mr. Good's "are not revilers before me?", Calmet's conditional turn, Coverdale's "I have deceived no man, yet must mine eye continue in heaviness" — before concluding, dryly, that the general meaning is plain enough and the reader has translations enough. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the sting the others only name: the friends abused Job with foul censures, mocking his calamities and insulting over him because he was brought low; they did all they could to provoke him and then condemned him for feeling it, so that his eye "continued in their provocation," never able to look off the wrong. It is the unkindness of those who trample on their friends in affliction, Henry says, that is enough to try, if not to tire, the patience even of Job himself. The witnesses do not divide over the substance — Job is mocked by the very men who came to mourn — however far apart their several renderings of the disputed Hebrew may stand.
3:
"Lay down now, put me in a surety with thee" — Job's plea for a pledge divides the witnesses over the one to whom it is addressed. The reformed John Gill takes it as spoken to God: "lay down now," or "put, I pray thee," a pledge that thou wilt provide a surety and admit one to plead for me, or else set thy heart and mind to my case and hear it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the same appeal more precise and more daring: Job asks God to be surety for him with himself. It is the very prayer of Hezekiah, "O Lord, I am oppressed; undertake for me," in Isa. 38:14, and of the psalmist, "be surety for thy servant for good," in Ps. 119:122. Job had longed for a daysman to lay his hand on both; now he longs for a surety that God alone can give, a witness of God to God himself — language, Ellicott marvels, that fits all we have since learned of the persons in the Godhead. "Who is he that will strike hands with me?" names the ancient gesture of becoming surety, and Job knows none of his friends will, or could.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, hears the words flung at the friends: "lay down now — deposit a pledge; stake your conduct against mine, and let the cause come before God, and see whether any of you shall be justified while I am condemned." On his reading the striking of hands is a wager thrown down to the accusers, not a plea lifted up to the Judge. John Wesley keeps to the appeal to God, glossing it as a humble desire that God would be his surety, or appoint him one to maintain his righteous cause against his opposers, "strike hands" being the usual gesture of the bargain.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the appeal into the confidence of a clear conscience: Job desires to be assured that God will take the hearing and determining of the cause into his own hands, for those whose hearts do not condemn them of reigning hypocrisy have this boldness toward God. And Henry records the reading of the English annotations that saw here a glance at the great Mediator — "appoint, I pray thee, my surety with thee, namely Christ, who is with thee in heaven, and has undertaken to be my surety" — so that the challenge "who is he then that will strike upon my hand?" becomes the believer's, none daring to lay anything to his charge if Christ be his advocate, as in Rom. 8:32-33. Christ is the surety of the better testament in Heb. 7:22. The witnesses part, then, over the hand Job reaches for — a wager to the friends or a surety from God — but agree that he has despaired of any earthly arbiter and cast his cause upon heaven.
4:
Job grounds his refusal to let his friends judge him in a stroke of God's own hand upon them, and the witnesses handle the hard saying "thou hast hid their heart from understanding." The reformed John Gill takes it as a real withholding: God had hidden understanding from the hearts of the three, so that they were unfit to be sureties or judges. This God sometimes does, Gill notes, in a natural sense, giving men up who like not the knowledge of him; and in a spiritual sense, hiding evangelical things from the wise and prudent; and even from his own people he sometimes hides the meaning of his providences, as he did from Asaph, from Jeremiah, from Habakkuk — and here from Job's friends, who therefore mistook his case.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is careful over the theology of the phrase. The address is to God, he says, and God is here represented as doing what in the course of his providence he only permits to be done; the hearts were hidden by being left to themselves. And Clarke reads the second clause, "therefore shalt thou not exalt them," as a prophecy exactly fulfilled: not one of Job's friends was exalted; on the contrary God condemned the whole of them, and they were not received again into favour until Job had sacrificed and made intercession for them. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, glosses the first clause bluntly — "thou hast blinded the minds of my friends, therefore I desire a wiser and abler judge" — and the second as a promise that God will not give them the victory in the contest but make them ashamed of their confidence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only the plain identification that anchors the whole, that "their heart" is the heart of the friends and no other; while Keil and Delitzsch, setting out their rendering of the strophe that runs from here through the perseverance of the righteous, take God without question as the subject of what follows, the one who has both darkened the friends and made Job a byword. The witnesses divide a little over the sense of "thou shalt not exalt them" — whether it foretells the friends' humbling at the book's end, as Clarke has it, or simply denies them the honour of carrying the argument, as Wesley reads it — but they agree on the sharp point Job is making: the men who have set themselves up to instruct him are, in this very matter, the ones from whom God has withheld the light. It is no light charge, that the very heart which should have judged his cause has been closed by the hand of the Judge himself.
5:
The verse is among the darkest cruxes in the chapter, three Hebrew words so brief, as one witness owns, that they are almost past construing, and the readings scatter widely. The reformed John Gill takes "he that speaketh flattery to his friends" of the comforters themselves, who flattered Job with promises of restored prosperity if he would but repent, or who spoke deceitfully for God in pressing that an afflicted man must be a hidden sinner; and the failing eyes of the children he reads as the curse such treachery entails. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reckons the friends among just such flatterers: they came to mourn, Eliphaz opened with commendation in ch. 4:3, and all promised him happiness on their terms, which Job now looks back on as flattery designed only to vex him the more.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses the great variety of meaning the terms will bear and reaches for the general sense: the man who expects much from his friends will be disappointed, and while he leans on them his children's eyes may fail looking for bread. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays the obscurity open. Literally, he says, the words run "for a portion he will tell friends," and what that means no one can be sure. Some render it "he denounceth his friends for a prey," a charge against the conduct of Job's friends toward him; others, "he would say, friends should take their part" — that is, any man who undertook to be Job's surety would look for the friends to share the burden, whereas, so far from that, the eyes of his sons would fail in the looking for it, and they would never see it.

So the verse yields no single confident reading, and the witnesses do not force one. What they hold in common is the drift, that a man betrayed by flatterers, or forsaken by friends who should have stood surety for him, entails a loss that reaches even to his children — whether the curse falls on the false friend's house, as Gill and Henry take it, or the disappointment on the deserted man's own, as Clarke and Ellicott read it. Job, having just called God to be his surety because no friend would strike hands with him, here measures how empty the friendship of flatterers proves in the day it is most needed. The obscurity of the Hebrew, far from emptying the line, only deepens the sense of a man groping among broken comforts for one that will hold; and the very brevity that baffles the grammarians answers, in its way, to the poverty of the consolation itself, so little and so dark that it can scarce be made to yield a meaning at all.
6:
"He hath made me also a byword of the people" — and the witnesses, having agreed that God is the unnamed maker of the reproach, divide sharply over the strange word rendered "tabret." The reformed John Gill notes that Job's very name has become a proverb ever since, whether for poverty or for patience; but here the byword is plainly to his reproach, the sort of thing men say of a wicked man or a hypocrite. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the taunt of a fallen favourite: they made ballads of him, his name became a proverb, "as poor as Job"; and "aforetime I was as a tabret" he takes two ways — either one played upon publicly, whom whoever chose might strike, or, in his prosperity, the very darling of the human race, the deliciae humani generis whom all were pleased with. It is common, Henry adds, for those honoured in their wealth to be despised in their poverty.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch will have nothing to do with the old guess that connected the word with Topheth and the fires of hell in the valley of Hinnom; "aforetime" cannot mean openly, they say, and the true root is tuph, to spit out, an onomatopoetic verb kin to the Greek and Latin words for spitting and to the German speien, and to the Arabic for treating with contempt. On their reading Job has become "one in whose face they spit." Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, offers the choice openly: either "I am become as a tabret, or drum, openly," a signal of warning, so that Job's case is fraught with warning for others, or else "an open abhorrence, one in whose face they spit."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes yet a third road. "Aforetime I was as a tabret" is not, he insists, the Hebrew at all; reading liphnehem for lephanim, he renders it "I shall be as a furnace, or consuming fire, before them," so that Job's example will one day be a fire to confound his false friends, who "shall have little reason to mock when they see the end of the Lord's dealings with me." So four readings of the one clause stand side by side — the darling once played on like a timbrel, the man spat upon, the drum of warning, and the consuming fire of vindication — and the witnesses do not pretend to reconcile them. They agree only on the first half, which needs no philology: that God has permitted a great and honoured man to become the common byword and jest of the people, a reproach in every mouth, so that the name once spoken with respect is now a thing to point at and to spit upon.
7:
From the reproach in every mouth Job passes to the visible ruin of his frame, and the witnesses read the two images of a dimmed eye and a shadowed body as the outward register of an inward grief. The reformed John Gill keeps to the plain cause: Job's eye is grown dim through excessive weeping, so many tears shed that his eyesight was well-nigh lost, or at the least greatly weakened and impaired. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that continual weeping impairs the sight, and indeed that any affliction which wastes the frame will weaken the eyes in the same measure; and he reads the second clause of a man reduced to nothing — "all my members are as a shadow" — with nothing left but skin and bone, the mere shadow of his former self.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers both clauses into a portrait of a man of sorrows. Job wept so much, he says, that he had almost lost his sight, as he had already owned in ch. 16:16; the sorrow of the world thus works darkness and death. And he had grieved so long that he had fretted all the flesh away and become a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones, so poor and thin that he was not to be called a man but the shadow of a man. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, laying out their rendering of the strophe, keep the same sense — "mine eye became dim with grief, and all my members were like a shadow" — before turning to the astonishment of the upright that the next verse will describe.

The witnesses do not divide; the verse is too plain in its pathos for dispute. What they draw from it together is the completeness of Job's undoing: the eye that was made to weep has wept itself half-blind, and the body that was lately vigorous is worn to a thin darkness cast upon the ground. It is the very picture of grief consuming the man who bears it — the outward frame answering, limb by wasted limb, to the terrors within — and it prepares the strange turn of the next verses, in which this ruined and shadowy sufferer becomes, against all likelihood, a spectacle from which the upright will take not despair but resolve. Job means the miserable inventory to aggravate his friends' unkindness and to justify his own complaint; but the witnesses hear in it more than self-pity, the honest reckoning of a man who will not pretend to a strength he no longer has, and who lays his wasted body open before God as part of the cause he means to plead.
8:
"Upright men shall be astonied at this" — the ruined sufferer becomes, unexpectedly, a sight that steadies rather than shakes the godly, and the witnesses trace how. The reformed John Gill reads the astonishment as the wonder of sincere and honourable men, then and in ages to come, that so good a man as Job should be so grievously afflicted in body, name, and estate, and that his own friends should add to his grief; it would be so surprising that they could scarce believe it, and more at a loss still how to account for it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry deepens the paradox: a remarkable saint proves a remarkable sufferer, so useful a man laid aside in the midst of his usefulness, and these are riddles that will not be unfolded till the mystery of God is finished. Yet the amazement, Henry says, does not deter the upright but animates them; "the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite," refusing to bear the profane inferences drawn from Job's case — that God has forsaken the earth, that it is vain to serve him — and standing up to withstand the scoffer to his face, for the boldness of the attacks upon religion should only sharpen the courage of its friends.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the verse prophetically. Adam Clarke takes Job to be speaking of the good his history will one day do: the upright will receive the account with astonishment and wonder at the dispensations of the Almighty, while hypocrites and false professors and the sour-minded godly are unmasked, and innocent men, whether in affliction or in affluence, are shown to be the favourites of heaven. John Wesley hears the upright "astonied at the depth and mysteriousness of God's judgments, which fall on innocent men while the worst of men prosper," and yet the more zealously opposing the hypocrites who make these strange providences an objection against religion itself.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the couplet its edge in translation — "the upright were astonished at it, and the innocent is stirred up over the godless" — and set over the whole the truth that governs the strophe: the truly righteous man, even if in the midst of his affliction he should see destruction before him, does not on that account forsake God. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job, at the very bottom of his misery, foresees that his case will not scandalize the faithful but rouse them, turning the offence of a suffering saint into a summons to hold the ground of religion against all who would make his affliction a weapon against God.
9:
The astonishment of the upright issues not in paralysis but in perseverance, and this verse — "the righteous also shall hold on his way" — is the one the witnesses read as the chapter's shaft of light. The reformed John Gill is careful to say who the righteous man is: not one righteous in mere appearance, but really so, justified by the righteousness of the living Redeemer Job had confessed, living by faith upon it and walking in holiness; and such a man will persevere. Gill sets the holding-on against every alternative — against going back, against turning to the right hand or the left, against standing still, stumbled and discouraged — and takes it to suppose a real progress, a pressing forward that neither the afflictions of himself or others, nor the reproaches of men, nor the temptations of Satan, nor seasons of darkness and desertion can move.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same resolve and the same growth. The righteous, far from drawing back or so much as standing still to deliberate at so frightful a spectacle, holds on his way with the more constancy; "though bonds and afflictions abide him, none of these things move him," as Paul said in Acts 20:24. And he not only holds on but grows stronger and stronger, made more vigorous by the sight of other good men's trials and the experience of his own — the blustering wind, Henry says, only makes the traveller gather his cloak the closer and gird it the faster. Those who keep their eye upon heaven as their end will keep their feet in the paths of religion as their way.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the verse the grand use of the whole book. There shall be no lasting doubt about the dispensations of Providence, he says; Job's case illustrates every seemingly partial display of God's government, so that none need be stumbled to see a godly man under oppression, for God permits it only for the good of the sufferer and the manifesting of his own mercy, wisdom, and love. The righteous man therefore takes it for granted that all is well managed and the end will be glorious, and by every blast of adversity he stays himself the more upon the Lord and gains strength. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, keep the plain triumph of the words — "the righteous holdeth fast on his way, and he that hath clean hands waxeth stronger and stronger." The witnesses do not divide; they stand together on the one verse in which Job, out of the depths, speaks not of the grave but of the road, and of the pilgrim who, seeing where it led even a saint, walks it the more boldly.
10:
Job wheels back upon his friends with something between a challenge and a dismissal — "but as for you all, do ye return, and come now" — and the witnesses weigh how much scorn is in it. The reformed John Gill hears a man confident of his cause daring all three to renew the dispute, three against one though they were; or else calling them to turn from their bad opinion and retract their hard censures, or at the least to sit down and hear him out. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes it as Job's verdict on their folly: "be convinced that you are in an error, for I cannot find one wise man among you" who knows how to explain the difficulties of God's providence or to apply the consolations of his promises. Those do not go wisely about the comforting of the afflicted, Henry adds, who fetch their comforts from the mere possibility of recovery in this world, which at best is uncertain; it is our wisdom to comfort ourselves and others with what cannot fail — the promise of God, his love and grace, and a well-grounded hope of eternal life.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the rebuke to its edge: the friends are too proud and self-important to profit by what they see, and Job bids them return — enter into themselves, consider their ways, go again to school and learn humility and knowledge — "for there is not one wise man among you." John Wesley reads the summons more evenly, as an invitation to renew the debate the friends were plainly resolved to renew in any case.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the irony that runs beneath the courtesy. "Come again and renew the argument," Job says in effect, "but I shall not be able to find a wise man among you"; he is willing to hear them out, yet already confident how the hearing must end. Ellicott fixes the last clause as a plain future — "and I shall not find," if ye do renew it — rather than a settled present verdict already passed. The witnesses divide only in temper, between Gill's open challenge, Henry's grave diagnosis of their failure as comforters, Clarke's stinging rebuke, and Ellicott's dry irony; on the substance they agree, that Job has weighed his three counsellors and found not one of them wise enough to speak to his case, so that he must carry it, as he has said all along, past them to God. The renewed invitation is thus no softening toward them, but a last exposure of how little help there was ever to be had from that quarter.
11:
Job sinks again from the challenge into the gloom that keeps returning upon him, and the witnesses read "my days are past, my purposes are broken off" as the collapse of every plan a prosperous man had laid. The reformed John Gill turns the first clause carefully: not that Job's days had outrun the bound God had fixed, for that no man passes, but that in his own apprehension the common term of his life was spent, so that it was folly in the friends to promise him length of days; or else that his good days, his days of prosperity, were past, and evil days come in which he had no pleasure. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it simply of the days of his life — "I am a dying man, and therefore the hopes you give me of the bettering of my condition are vain" — and takes the broken purposes to be those he had formed in his prosperous days concerning himself and his children.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lets the verse open all that Job had once designed. He had pleased himself with projects and prospects — of enlarging his border, increasing his stock, settling his children, and many a pious thought besides, of promoting religion in his country, redressing grievances, reforming the profane, relieving the poor; and now he concludes that all these thoughts of his heart are at an end, dashed and cut off. The period of our days, Henry observes, will be the period of all our contrivances and hopes for this world; and yet, he adds, if with full purpose of heart we cleave to the Lord, death will not break off that purpose.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the broken purposes as "the cherished thoughts of my heart" cut off — the very possessions, as it were, of the inner man — and carry the sentence straight on into the friends' false comfort of the next verse. The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, hears in the whole a relapse into gloom, and reflects on the frequency of just such transitions in the poem, which mark the struggle of piety and resignation with continued affliction and gloomy providence; all Job's purposes, he says, are interrupted, his schemes and plans for himself and his family torn asunder. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse is the sound of a life's designs breaking off short against the fact of approaching death, and that only the purpose which is fixed on God survives the breaking. What the friends offered as a future, Job answers, has no ground to stand on, for the man they would rebuild has already, in his own eyes, run out his days.
12:
The broken purposes leave Job's nights as comfortless as his days, and over the strange line "they change the night into day" the witnesses divide chiefly over who "they" are. The reformed John Gill offers both hands. It may be Job's own thoughts, so busy in the night season upon what had been said in the day that he could get no sleep and the night became as broad day to him; or it may be the friends, who put the day before the night against the order of nature, promising him long days brighter than the noon, as in ch. 11:17, when in truth the night of death was coming on. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley leans to the first: his thoughts so incessantly pursue and disturb him that he can no more sleep by night than by day, and the daylight that gives other men in misery some comfort seems gone as soon as it is begun, because of the pains that follow him about.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott leans to the second, and reads the verse as a bitter comment on the friends' failure to enter into his case. So little did they understand him that they would have him believe his night of trial was the very reverse of darkness, with light at hand — "the light," they say, "is near unto the darkness," near before ever the darkness comes; they try to persuade him that prosperity is close by. To Job, whose felt condition was all darkness, this was only the more painful mockery.

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, takes the disputed second clause more inwardly still. "The light is short because of darkness" he renders "the light is near from the face of darkness": Job has scarcely any light, and what he has is so near akin to the dark that it is hardly severed from it — a darkness made just visible, a fine picture, Clarke says, of a mind generally overcast but crossed now and then by a gleam of hope. The witnesses part, then, over the subject and the shading of the line — whether it is Job's sleepless thoughts or his friends' false promises that turn night into day, and whether the little light is their flattering dawn or his own faint glimmer — but they meet in the sense of a man for whom the natural comforts of night and morning alike have failed, so that rest and daylight have changed places and both are lost.
13:
If Job is to wait for any home, it is for one of a very different sort than the friends have promised, and the witnesses gather about the words "the grave is mine house." The reformed John Gill is at pains to say that Job casts no "if" upon waiting on God, in which he was resolved to persevere; the condition is set against the friends' counsel. They had intimated that on repentance he might look for a peaceable tabernacle and a prosperous habitation; but should he listen, Gill says, and put himself in a waiting posture for such small things, how soon would it be over, for what house can he rationally expect but the grave, man's long home? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way: were he to wait for deliverance he would be disappointed, being already upon the borders of the grave; he expects no rest but the dark grave, and prepares himself for it — endeavouring to make the bed easy by keeping his conscience pure, by seeing Christ lying in it and so turning it into a bed of spices, and by looking beyond it to the resurrection.

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, states it barely: let his life be long or short, the grave at last will be his home, where he shall soon lie down in darkness, and he can reasonably hope for nothing else. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, however, dwells on the grave until he has almost made it welcome. Job counts upon no house but this one: "if there be any place where I shall ever be easy again, it must be in the grave." And Henry turns the thought over tenderly — the grave is a house, to the wicked a prison-house, as in ch. 24:19-20, but to the godly a passage-house on the way home; "it is my house, mine by descent, my father's house, and mine by purchase." It is a bed, too, where the saints rest in the evening of their day on earth and rise in the morning of their everlasting day, as in Isa. 57:2; and this, Henry says, should make good people willing to die, for it is but going to bed when one is weary and it is time.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job's settled reckoning that the only home and the only rest now before him is the grave — a reckoning the friends called despair, but which the godly witnesses turn into a kind of hope, since the bed is made in darkness only to be risen from in light. Job, having refused their painted future, chooses instead to make his peace with the one dwelling he is sure of, and even there the witnesses will not let the darkness be the last word.
14:
Job carries the household imagery down into the grave itself, greeting corruption and the worm as his nearest kin, and the witnesses feel both the horror and the strange intimacy of it. The reformed John Gill will not let "corruption" mean the corruptible seed of his begetting nor the purulent matter of his boils, but the corruption his body must turn to in the grave — the "pit of corruption," where the dead putrefy. As in a house there dwell together father and mother, brother and sister, in loving familiarity, so in the grave, the dwelling-house of all men, corruption and rottenness, dust and worms, are the household; and with these Job claims kindred, speaking to them not only familiarly but respectfully. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same picture: Job cries to corruption, "thou art my father," for our bodies were formed out of the earth, and to the worms, "you are my mother and my sister," for man is a worm and the worms shall cover us, as in ch. 21:26. Job's own kindred had estranged themselves from him, Henry recalls from ch. 19:13-14, and so he claims here the relations that will cleave to him when those disown him. We are all near akin to corruption and the worms, Henry says, and it is good to make ourselves familiar with them in our thoughts, that we may be lifted above the inordinate love of life and the fear of death.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of a man owning his origin and his end at once: "I came from a corrupted stock, and I must go to corruption again"; the Hebrew he would render "to the ditch I have called, Thou art my father; to the worm, Thou art my mother and my sister," Job being now in the nearest state of affinity to dissolution, so that he may well call these his nearest relations. John Wesley glosses "corruption" as "the pit of corruption, the grave," and hears in "thou art my father" the confidence of a child: "I am near akin to thee, and thou wilt receive and keep me in thy house, as parents do their children."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the cry in their rendering — "I cry to corruption: Thou art my father; to the worm: Thou art my mother and sister" — the address of a man who has made the grave his family. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse neither blasphemy nor mere morbidity but a dreadful acceptance, Job embracing decay as kindred because he has nothing else left to embrace, and finding in that grim household a familiarity that reconciles him to the death he can no longer escape.
15:
"And where is now my hope?" — the cry seems to cancel everything, and the witnesses are careful to say what hope Job means and what he does not. The reformed John Gill draws the distinctions firmly. Job does not mean the grace of hope that was in his heart, for that is an anchor sure and steadfast and can never be lost; nor the object of that hope, the eternal glory laid up in heaven, for which he still looked by faith. He means the hope of outward happiness, of being restored to his former prosperity or a better, which his friends had pressed upon him; and this, Gill says, had no place in him now, for all ground and foundation of it was removed. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley puts it in a phrase — the hope in question is "the happiness you would have me expect" — and Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, asks in the same key: in the circumstances Job is found in, of what use can such hope be? Were he to form any expectation of future good, who could ever see it realized? and is it any wonder, then, that he complains of his wretched lot?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds the two hopes apart most sharply of all. Seeing he must shortly leave the world, Job asks how he can expect to prosper who does not expect to live; yet he is not hopeless, only his hope is not where his friends would place it. "If in this life only I had hope, I were of all men most miserable" — but his hope is out of sight: "who shall see it? It is something out of sight that I hope for, not the things that are seen, which are temporal, but the things not seen, which are eternal." What that hope is, Henry says, Job will tell in ch. 19:25, the living Redeemer; here he only distinguishes it from the perishing comforts the friends offer, seeking not that which perishes but that which abides for ever.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job has buried one hope and not another: the hope of restored fortune is gone with his health and his estate, but the hope that reaches past the grave he does not so much as question — he only insists that no eye of his friends will ever see the earthly recovery they keep dangling before him. It is a fine and deliberate distinction, and the witnesses make much of it, for it keeps the darkest verse of the chapter from being read as the despair it sounds: the man who asks "where is my hope?" has not lost hope itself, but only the counterfeit his comforters kept pressing on him in its place.
16:
The chapter ends on its hardest verse, "they shall go down to the bars of the pit," and the witnesses close both with an image and with a frank confession of difficulty. The reformed John Gill reads it of Job, his friends, and the hopes they urged, all going down together to the grave to lie barred and locked up there, the hopes never to rise and the bodies to wait until he who has the keys of death shall loose them; or else, taking "the bars" as the subject, of the members of the body — the bones that are its bars and stays — going down to the grave to turn to rottenness and dust, so that Job may ask again, what is my strength, that I should hope? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley notes that Job speaks of his hope in the singular in the verse before and here shifts to the plural, as the poetical books often do; the "bars" he takes for the innermost parts of the pit, into which his dying hopes descend to be buried with him. We must all shortly be under the bars of the pit, Wesley adds, held fast till the general resurrection, where all good men, if they cannot agree now, will rest together — a foresight that should cool the heat of all contenders.

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, plays over the word "bars," which may also mean branches or distended limbs or claws, and pictures either the grave as a monster gripping human bodies fast in its deadly hold, or the branching alleys of a catacomb with their niches for the dead; when he and his hope have their rest together in the dust, it will never be realized. And Clarke lingers on the shadow that lay over such minds, for whom the state of man after death was full of perplexity, the true light not yet come until Jesus brought life and immortality to light.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns this to be the most difficult verse of a difficult chapter, and lays the knot open: "the bars of the pit" are masculine, but the verb "they shall go down" is feminine plural, so that the bars can hardly be its subject, and yet "hope," the apparent subject, is feminine singular and will not agree either. Some render "it shall go down," in defiance of the grammar, and though the rule that a verb before its subject need not agree with it might help, here the verb must follow its subject, and the only subject in sight — the corruption and the worm of v.14 — are already in the grave, not going down to it. Ellicott does not force a solution; he leaves the words as a plain cry of utter despair, that Job's only rest is in the dust. The witnesses do not finally divide; whatever the disputed grammar yields, they read the close as it stands, a man laying his last hopes down with his body in the grave, and finding there, as the godly among them insist, not the end of all things but the bed from which the buried are one day raised.
